name: glktermw
desc: Terminal-window Glk library with Unicode support
why: A Glk terminal implementation lets classic Interactive Fiction like Zork-style Infocom games run in a terminal with Unicode.

brief.what_it_is: glktermw is a Glk library for Unix terminals, built on GlkTerm 1.0.4 and modified by Alexander Beels to accept and display Unicode characters through ncursesw. Glk is an interface standard for interactive fiction. A Glk program calls the library's windowing, text input and output functions, and glktermw draws those windows in a terminal and passes keystrokes back. The homepage is the Glk specification page rather than a page for glktermw, so the package-specific details below come from the IF Archive listing and the homepage's own description of the Unicode port.
brief.why_it_exists: Glk exists so that interactive fiction interpreters and games can be written once against a standard API and then run on many platforms, each with its own Glk library. The homepage describes Glk as 'a free standard' and says that 'If you're going to run a Glk program, you need a Glk library which runs on your machine.' glktermw fills the terminal slot and adds Unicode.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes GlkTerm as 'implemented using the curses.h screen control library', and says the wide-char version is 'modified to use ncursesw or ncurses to display and accept all Unicode characters which the terminal supports.' The Glk spec adds that Unicode text files must be UTF-8. A Glk game is compiled or linked against the library, and the library handles the terminal.
brief.install_notes: Homepage gives no install commands. It says the library should compile on Unix systems that have curses.h, and the Unicode version needs ncursesw or ncurses. The IF Archive lists the source as glktermw-104.tar.gz, so installation is a source build from that tarball; no binary package or brew-specific steps appear in what I read. Brew reports no executables for this formula, so it installs a library, not a runnable game. You need a separate Glk program, such as a Glk-based interpreter or game, to run anything.
brief.standout: Unlike most terminal IF tools, this is a library for a shared interface standard. Any Glk-compliant game or interpreter can run on it without changes. The Unicode port is a single community patch on an older library, which makes it an unusual piece of IF plumbing.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says of the wide-char GlkTerm port: 'No longer supported.' The IF Archive file glktermw-104.tar.gz is dated 14-Oct-2012, which is the most recent upload I could see for it. The Glk spec itself is maintained: the homepage was last updated June 2, 2025, and the spec is at version 0.7.6.
brief.caveats: The upstream note says the wide-char GlkTerm port is no longer supported, and the base GlkTerm 1.0.4 is also unsupported and targets Glk 0.7.4 rather than the current 0.7.6. Platform is Unix-like systems with curses or ncursesw. The scout note says it runs 'Zork-style Infocom games'. The homepage does not say that. It lists Dungeon 3.2B for Glk, Nitfol and Zeal (Z-machine interpreters), and Glulx, which are Glk programs, so Infocom-style games are plausible, but the connection is an inference. Dungeon 3.2B is the Fortran lineage that Zork came from, not Zork itself. Licence terms were not visible in what I read.
quotes: Should compile on any Unix system or reasonable facsimile, as long as it has the curses.h library.
Alexander Beels has contributed a port of GlkTerm which can accept and display Unicode characters, using the ncursesw library.
